title: First Thing: Blockbuster Anthropic IPO fails to halt global slide in AI stocks
summary:
Record-breaking IPO for company behind Claude comes amid tumbling prices for other AI stocks. Plus why the humble potato could be vital for future space missions

Good morning.

blocks.text: Good morning. Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies. The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by over 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

The blockbuster debut easily places Anthropic’s IPO as the biggest in history, with the 980m shares sold raising $81bn, surpassing the previous record. According to reports, demand for Anthropic shares was about six times what the company was able to offer. US economic growth is inextricably tied to the booming AI sector, and in particular the vast investments in datacentres that power programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

Senior Democrats have already suggested that tech companies could face a regulatory crackdown over the dangers that advanced AI models pose, and over the volatility that AI IPOs could introduce into the economy.

items: Who has been made wealthy by Anthropic’s IPO? Dan Milmo and Aisha Down profile the seven co-founders of the company who are now worth $180bn – with physicists, a former journalist and an associate of the pope among the company’s guiding lights.

How has the White House responded to the recent spate of tech failures? The White House national ⁠cyber director, Sean ⁠Cairncross, ​has been ousted from his job, days after tech outages hit US air travel, banking and national security systems. The Department of Defense chief information officer, ​Kirsten Davies, will ‌assume the position ‌temporarily.

blocks.text: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling

blocks.caption: Rohingya refugees watch the ruling from a camp in Bangladesh. Photograph: Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The US has reacted with caution to the world’s highest court ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority. The historic ruling from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – could set a precedent.

The court recognised that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh. In this analysis piece, the Guardian’s senior international correspondent Julian Borger explains why the ruling gives new relevance to the genocide convention and is “full of messages” for other states accused of genocide, notably Israel.

items: How have the scattered communities of Rohingya reacted to the judgment? There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh. Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, said: “Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice”. But she does not expect to be able to return home; her village was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists.

blocks.text: Senate Republicans reject war powers bill to halt fighting in Iran

blocks.caption: A school damaged in an attack by the US in Minab. Photograph: Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Senate on Thursday rejected a war powers resolution aimed at forcing Donald Trump to halt fighting with Iran, with Republicans once again defending a conflict that played a major role in their sweeping midterm election losses. The House of Representatives had approved the resolution in September. The measure failed in a 48-51 vote that broke largely along party lines.
Religious messages US agriculture secretary emailed to staff deemed unconstitutional

blocks.caption: Brooke Rollins. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

blocks.text: Religious messages that the US agriculture secretary, Brooke Rollins, emailed to the agency’s 100,000 employees were unconstitutional, and she must be careful to avoid proselytizing when communicating with workers, a federal judge ruled on Thursday.

Employees cannot realistically opt out of reading emails from their agency director, and the messages could coerce them to hide their own faith or feel pressure to adopt Rollins’s Christian faith, the judge ruled.
Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping’s speech at Apec summit in China

blocks.caption: A still from a video appears to show Trump asleep. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China. White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him. You can judge for yourself in this video clip.
In other news …

items: Thomas Markle, the 82-year-old estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, has been ruled mentally competent to face charges of keeping child sexual abuse material in storage in California.
Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein.

Trump’s DoJ has moved to drop its legal challenge to Mary Peltola’s Alaska Senate win. The president had sought to block the results if the Democrat won a race that featured two candidates named Dan Sullivan.
Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died. Efforts to remove a knitted hat that she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure proved unsuccessful.
The US army has delayed its plan to detonate a stash of bomb-making chemicals in south-eastern Iowa as questions swirl about the public health risks.
A joint European-Japanese space mission has arrived at Mercury on only the second-ever mission to enter its orbit.
The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.

blocks.text: Stat of the day: Suspects charged in California train heist ring that netted cargo worth $22m

blocks.caption: Containers are transported by trains and trucks from the Long Beach terminal in California. Photograph: Damian Dovarganes/AP

blocks.text: More than a dozen people were charged on Thursday with allegedly orchestrating a vast train heist operation to steal more than $22m in cargo from major retailers.
Culture pick: Tarantino and Fincher join forces for Brad Pitt’s glorious return

blocks.caption: Brad Pitt in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Photograph: Netflix/AP

blocks.text: David Fincher directs Quentin Tarantino’s script, picking up from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, and Peter Bradshaw says its lead is more ineffably beguiling than ever in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.
Don’t miss this: Outcry after US holds first deep-sea mining lease sale near American Samoa

blocks.caption: Children play on a raft near Pago Pago, American Samoa. Photograph: Annika Hammerschlag/AP

blocks.text: Mar-Vic Cagurangan reports from Guam that the US has carried out its first ever deep-sea mining lease sales off the coast of American Samoa, despite an adverse court ruling earlier this week and mounting local opposition.
Climate check: Native communities in US south-west try to recover after flooding intensified by El Niño

blocks.caption: Flooding in Shiprock, New Mexico. Photograph: Navajo Police Department

blocks.text: Cecilia Nowell has been in Shiprock, where residents and local groups have banded together after severe flooding submerged a New Mexico town in toxic water.

items: Follow the latest from Cop31 as climate talks enter their final scheduled day with our live blog.

blocks.text: Last Thing: Scientists say potatoes could be key food source for a moon base

blocks.caption: Vintage 1980s space Lego. Photograph: Martin Belam/The Guardian

blocks.text: Growing the humble potato on the moon could be the key to sustaining human life there on future space missions, according to a new scientific report.
